title: NoSQL: choosing a model for the system requirements
lead: A product name cannot answer the essential questions: how fresh must the data be, how will the application access it, and how should the system handle failures?
goals: Explain the trade-off during a network partition.
Compare key-value, document, column-family, and graph data models.

sections.title: Separate two design decisions
sections.html:
Sharding divides the data; replication creates copies of the data. A system can use both. A flexible schema does not mean the data has no structure. Structural checks may instead be performed by application code or configured validation rules.

NoSQL describes a family of approaches. The label does not imply that every NoSQL system lacks transactions or that every relational database is unable to scale. Examine a system's specific guarantees rather than relying on the SQL or NoSQL label.

Source: PDF pages 1–8. The examples and explanations on this learning page were written independently for this learning companion.

Capacity is not the same as query efficiency

Vertical scaling gives one node more resources; horizontal scaling adds nodes. The useful choice depends on working-set size, query fan-out, skew, cross-shard transactions, replication and coordination. Relational systems can distribute work too. Sharding does not make cross-shard transactions impossible, but implementing their guarantees has a cost.

Original capacity example. Divide 300 GB of logical data evenly into three 100 GB shards. With two total copies of each shard, the raw data copies consume 600 GB before indexes, logs or overhead. A key lookup can route to one shard and a suitable replica; an all-category query may need every shard. Additional copies can lag and need an update policy; they are not new logical records.

Exercise: does doubling replicas double the logical query's row count?

Worked answer. No. Replication changes physical copies and potential service capacity, not the logical dataset. More replicas may improve reads or fault tolerance, but also add update and coordination work.

Audit addition: original explanation and worked example. Related evidence: Lecture source · physical PDF pages 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

sections.title: A network partition and a stale read
sections.html:
Two regions, E and W, both store a price of 50. The connection between them fails, leaving no path for exchanging information. This is a network partition, even though the nodes themselves are still running. E accepts a write that changes the price to 60 and reports success. After that write completes, a user in W starts reading the price.

  • If W returns the old price of 50, the system violates linearizability. The write completed before the read began, so the read must return 60, assuming there are no later writes.
  • If W waits for information from E, an indefinitely long partition may prevent the request from ever completing successfully. Rejecting the request also fails to provide availability in the CAP sense.

In CAP, C means linearizability: operations appear to execute against a single copy and respect real-time ordering. A requires every request to a non-failing node eventually to receive a valid result. It does not merely mean responding quickly or returning an error code. During a partition, a system cannot guarantee both C and A for every possible execution.

Key takeaway

CAP concerns the guarantees a system can provide when communication is disrupted by a partition. It is not a rule that lets a system freely choose any two of three properties at all times. CAP consistency also differs from ACID consistency, which concerns data invariants.

In this example, neither E nor W has failed. The problem is that W lacks information about a write that has already succeeded. Waiting for communication to recover can preserve C, but cannot guarantee A if the partition never ends.

Source: PDF pages 9–11. The examples and explanations on this learning page were written independently for this learning companion.

CAP clarification: Gilbert & Lynch, original definitions and theorem.

A guarantee quantifies over the permitted executions

The formal CAP impossibility concerns read/write behavior under a communication partition. Linearizability must hold for every history permitted by the claimed guarantee, and availability requires each request at a non-failing node to complete with an operation result. An arbitrary refusal/error is not a successfully served read or write merely because a network response arrived. The trade-off is exposed by some permitted partitioned executions, not a prediction that every request in every partition must fail.

A network partition is communication loss, whereas sharding is data placement. Outside partitioned executions, the theorem does not forbid providing both linearizable consistency and availability. The original Gilbert–Lynch definitions and theorem are attached directly to the five CAP bank questions so the precise clarification has its own primary evidence alongside the lecture pages.

Audit addition: original explanation and worked example. Related evidence: Lecture source · physical PDF pages 9, 10; Primary CAP definitions · physical PDF pages 2, 3, 4.

sections.title: BASE and application requirements
sections.html:
Eventual consistency means that replicas eventually converge if no new updates occur and data exchange eventually succeeds. It does not promise that every read immediately after a write will see the new value.

Consider the application requirements: an article's view count can often lag by a few seconds, while selling the same last available seat to two customers is usually unacceptable. For a shopping cart, the system needs an explicit merge policy. If two locations each add a different item, should the merged cart retain both? The word “eventual” does not specify how conflicts are resolved.

Key takeaway

Eventual consistency promises convergence under appropriate conditions. By itself, it does not promise immediate visibility of the latest write, a bound on convergence time, or a particular rule for merging concurrent updates.

Source: PDF pages 11–14. The examples and explanations on this learning page were written independently for this learning companion.

Expand BASE without overclaiming

Basically Available describes a design aim of serving useful requests under the system's chosen failure and consistency policies; the acronym is not a proof that every request succeeds in every execution. Soft State allows a node's state to change through replication or background processing without a new client write there. Eventual Consistency describes convergence when updates stop and the required propagation/progress conditions hold.

Original profile example. East accepts a profile change and later propagation updates West without a new West client request: this illustrates soft state. West may read an older profile during the delay. That visibility delay differs from losing an acknowledged committed update after failure, which is a durability problem. Specify the merge/conflict rule and the freshness requirement rather than treating “eventual” as a deadline.

Exercise: does eventual convergence tell you which simultaneous cart update wins?

Worked answer. No. A system still needs a conflict-resolution rule, such as a suitable merge or explicitly defined winner policy. Convergence alone neither chooses that rule nor promises immediate read-your-writes behavior.

Audit addition: original explanation and worked example. Related evidence: Lecture source · physical PDF pages 8, 9, 11.

sections.title: Four models and the questions they answer
sections.html:
• Key-value: Retrieve a blob using a session ID. This works well when the exact key is known.
  • Document: Store products with varying attributes and arrays, and filter on fields inside each document.
  • Column-family: Organize many sparse fields around keys and access patterns. Do not confuse this model with columnar storage for OLAP.
  • Graph: Represent people, accounts, and relationships, and query paths, connections, or patterns between them.

Consider this JSON example: {"sku":"P7","tags":["blue","small"],"spec":{"weight":2}}. Nested objects and arrays differ from a flat table, but they can be mapped to relations. The trade-offs involve access patterns, updates, and constraints.

Source: PDF pages 12–19. The examples and explanations on this learning page were written independently for this learning companion.

An opaque value makes the key-value contract clear

The basic key-value interface provides get, put and delete by key; it treats a value as opaque payload. Searching inside every profile for age>25 needs client-side processing or an additional indexing/query API. Actual products may provide those extra capabilities, so this basic model is not a claim that every key-value product lacks them.

A placement hash and its replica-placement functions can send copies of one item to different failure domains. Distinguish hashing the key for routing from hashing inside a local data structure. Multiple replicas still represent one logical item. An acknowledgment at replica A followed by a delayed update at B may permit an older read at B under an eventual-consistency policy; the exact visibility promise depends on the configured protocol.

Exercise: is get('user:7') equivalent to “find every user older than 25”?

Worked answer. No. The first names one exact key; the second is a field predicate over many values and needs another mechanism. Choosing a data model begins with the access pattern.

Audit addition: original explanation and worked example. Related evidence: Lecture source · physical PDF pages 12, 14.

Objects, arrays and validation have different roles

JSON objects associate field names with values, and arrays are ordered sequences that can contain nested values. Self-describing structure does not establish agreed field meanings, validation rules, transactions or concurrency semantics. A document such as a product with optional specifications still needs a policy for required fields and units.

Original predicate example. Three documents have names An, Bo and Cy with ages 25, 26 and 30. The strict predicate age>25 returns Bo and Cy; age≥25 also returns An. Arrays ["a","b"] and ["b","a"] have different order even when they contain the same two strings. Relational systems can store/query JSON through supported facilities; JSON does not determine one exclusive DBMS family.

Exercise: do flexible documents remove the need to agree whether age is numeric?

Worked answer. No. Validation or application rules must define the expected type and meaning. Structural flexibility is independent of the guarantees for an atomic multi-document update.

Audit addition: original explanation and worked example. Related evidence: Lecture source · physical PDF pages 15, 16, 17, 21.

Choose the relationship pattern, not just a graph label

A property graph represents entities as nodes, relationships as edges, and properties on either. In an original example, An —FRIEND→ Bo —FRIEND→ Cy yields Cy in an exact two-hop outgoing FRIEND query from An. An —DRIVES→ Car7 is a different edge label, so it contributes neither Cy nor Car8 to that FRIEND pattern. A path's direction and label are part of its meaning.

Audit addition: original explanation and worked example. Related evidence: Lecture source · physical PDF pages 13, 18, 19.

sections.title: Practice choosing a design
sections.html:
A shop has a frequently changing product catalog, a checkout process that requires consistent inventory, and a relationship-based recommendation system. These three workloads do not have to use the same data model. Write down their requirements separately: catalog lookups and filtering, atomic reservations, and graph traversal.

A good answer explains the cost of synchronizing the components rather than merely naming three products. The popularity chart in the PDF is a snapshot from March 2026. It is neither a performance benchmark nor a current recommendation. GQL, Cypher, and SPARQL represent graph-query language families; the choice should match the actual data model.

Source: PDF pages 18–21. The examples and explanations on this learning page were written independently for this learning companion.

Graph language names need their data-model context

Cypher and GQL are associated with property-graph queries; SQL/PGQ brings property-graph querying into SQL; SPARQL works with RDF/semantic-web data. These contexts help interpret the lecture's examples without asserting any unverified standard date or universal syntax compatibility. A traversal query and an aggregate over all nodes can favor different physical designs even within the same graph product.

Exercise: should every outgoing edge from An count as a friendship?

Worked answer. No. The FRIEND label excludes the DRIVES relationship. Query constraints, including edge direction and length, determine the match; merely sharing a starting node is insufficient.

Audit addition: original explanation and worked example. Related evidence: Lecture source · physical PDF pages 13, 18, 19.

Keep popularity evidence in its historical scope

The lecture's March 2026 table places Oracle first and labels MongoDB “Document, Multi-model”. These are facts about that source snapshot, not claims about today's ranking or an experimental performance result. Popularity signals cannot establish a system's latency, transaction semantics or fitness for one application. A product can support more than one data model.

For the shop example, field-based catalog queries, an atomic inventory reservation and recommendation traversal are distinct requirements. One multi-model system or multiple synchronized systems can be reasonable, with different operational and coordination costs. A recommendation that lags by a minute can be acceptable under a stated requirement; the checkout must use its authoritative inventory protocol to avoid overselling.

Exercise: two buyers see one item in a stale recommendation cache. How should checkout reserve it?

Worked answer. Use an authoritative atomic conditional reservation or an appropriate transaction/protocol that prevents both buyers from consuming the same remaining unit. A fresh-looking cache value and a popular product name do not enforce that invariant. Evaluate the chosen system's actual guarantees.

Audit addition: original explanation and worked example. Related evidence: Lecture source · physical PDF pages 20, 21.

quiz.question: Two replicas cannot communicate, and one has acknowledged a new write. What is the problem if a later read at the other replica immediately returns the old value?
options: It does not preserve linearizable consistency.
It cannot be a NoSQL system.
quiz.explanation: A read that starts after a successful write but returns the old value does not satisfy linearizability. This is the central trade-off illustrated by CAP.

source.summary: Lecture 27 covers the motivation for NoSQL, sharding and replication, CAP and BASE, data models, and workload-driven choices. This learning material also explains how to interpret simplified CAP diagrams carefully.
